# Why computational biology? {background-color="#1b3a5c"}

## Origins of Comp Bio

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

-   Fred Sanger seqeunced first protein (insulin) in 1952

-   Margaret Dayhoff & colleagues stored protein sequence data in the Protein
    Information Resource (1960s & 70s)

-   1960s: Dayhoff, Cavalli-Sforza & Edwards use computers to infer phylogenies

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

![Margaret Dayhoff](
    ../images/dayhoff.jpg
){
    fig-align="center"
    fig-alt="Picture of Margaret Dayhoff"
}

![McLaughlin & Dayhoff 1973^[@McLaughlinDayhoff1973]](
    ../images/mclaughlin-dayhoff-1973-tree.png
){
    fig-align="center"
    fig-alt="Phylogeny of eukaryotes"
}

:::
:::


## Biology became a data science

::: {.incremental}
- One human genome: ~3.1 billion base pairs
- One MiSeq run: tens of millions of reads
- GenBank, SRA, UniProt, PDB: petabytes, doubling every couple of years
- Sequencing costs have fallen faster than computing has gotten cheaper
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
The bottleneck in modern biology is rarely *generating* data.
It is deciding what to **do** with it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask: how long would it take to read 3 billion characters at 200 words/min?
Roughly 100+ years without sleeping. This is not a "work harder" problem.
:::

## Example 1 — Reading a genome you never see

You sequence a bacterial isolate and get back 4 million short reads,
each ~150 bp, in random order, with errors.

. . .

**The question:** what is the genome?

. . .

**The problem:** this is a jigsaw puzzle with millions of pieces, no picture on
the box, some pieces duplicated, and some pieces wrong.

. . .

Nobody solves this by hand. An *assembly algorithm* does — by building a graph
of overlapping *k*-mers and finding a path through it.

::: {.notes}
Don't explain de Bruijn graphs. The point is: a well-posed biological question
becomes a computational object (a graph) with a procedure attached.
:::

## Example 2 — Pathogen surveillance in real time

During SARS-CoV-2, sequences were deposited daily and phylogenies were rebuilt
continuously to track which lineages were spreading where.

. . .

That pipeline is a stack of algorithms:

::: {.incremental}
- align millions of genomes to a reference
- infer a tree relating them
- map the tree onto geography and time
:::

. . .

If the tree takes six weeks to compute, the answer is useless.
**Speed is not a convenience here — it is the whole point.**

## The takeaway

> A biological question becomes a computational question when we have to specify
> **exactly how** to get from data to answer.


## Comp Bio is also a mindset

![](
    ../images/transcription-factor.png
){
    fig-align="center"
    fig-alt="Diagram of transcription factor binding DNA to initiate transcription"
}

**Biology**: GATGAG sequence is necessary and sufficient to induce expression

. . .

**Comp Bio**:
-   What is the probability of TF binding given GATGAG sequence? — $P$(TF binding | GATGAG)
-   What is the probability of gene expression? — $P$(Gene x expression | GATGAG & TF)

. . .

Biology isn't black & white: Think probabilistically using models!


# Intro to Python {background-color="#1b3a5c"}

## What is Python?

It's a programming language that is
<ul>
	<li class="fragment fade-up">Interpreted</li>
	<li class="fragment fade-up">Largely procedural, but flexible</li>
	<li class="fragment fade-up">Terse and clear</li>
    <ul>
	    <li class="fragment fade-up">"Pseudocode that works"</li>
    </ul>
	<li class="fragment fade-up">Comes with standard libraries for interacting with the OS</li>
	<li class="fragment fade-up">Diverse, stable libraries for work across many domains</li>
	<li class="fragment fade-up">Industry standard in many fields: Machine learning, data science</li>
</ul>

## What is a Python notebook?

::: {.incremental}
-   An interactive web-based document that allows you to combine runnable
    Python code, formatted text, and visualizations in one place.
-   Composed of modular building blocks called "cells"
    -   Instead of running a whole script of Python code, snippets of code in
        each cell run individually
:::

## Types of cells

::: {.incremental}
Code (Python) cells
:   Snippets of Python code that run individually; output of code appears underneath the cell   

Markdown cells:
:   Formatted text and images created using Markdown syntax; used to explain/document the code
:::

## What is marimo?

-   One type of Python notebook
-   Jupyter is another type that is more popular

. . .

So, why marimo?

## Why marimo?

IMHO, marimo solved two big problems with other types of notebooks:

::: {.incremental}
-   Results can vary depending on the order cells are run
    -   marimo soflves this by being "**reactive**"

-   The plain text files of other notebooks are illegible (nested in JSON syntax)
    -   marimo is pure Python
:::

## What is molab?

::: {.incremental}
-   A free, cloud-hosted workspace for running marimo Python notebooks
-   The name is a play on Google colab, a popular service for Jypyter notebooks
-   It will be our primary means of practicing comp bio
:::

## Ten simple rules for biologists learning to program^[@Carey2018]

::: {.incremental}
1.  Begin with the end in mind
2.  Baby steps are steps
3.  Immersion is the best learning tool
4.  Phone a friend
5.  Learn how to ask questions
6.  Don’t reinvent the wheel
7.  Develop good habits early on
8.  Practice makes perfect
9.  Teach yourself
10. Just do it
:::
